title: Redirecting childhood feelings onto the therapist: transference
vignette: A 48-year-old man begins psychotherapy due to depression and escalating conflicts with his boss. He makes progress in the therapy sessions and reports feeling less depressed. The patient has also reflected on how his father was rarely available during his childhood and prioritized work over spending time with him. The following week, the psychiatrist unexpectedly cancels a session to attend to a family emergency. At the next appointment, the psychiatrist apologizes for canceling the last session. The patient replies, "You aren't there when I need you because I'm not important to you." Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's reaction to the psychiatrist?

clues.text: his father was rarely available during his childhood
clues.note: Early attachment experiences with an unavailable father are the source of feelings that get reactivated in the present relationship.

clues.text: You aren't there when I need you because I'm not important to you
clues.note: The patient projects childhood feelings of abandonment by his father onto the psychiatrist - a present-day person - which is transference.

whatMatters: TRANSFERENCE is the unconscious redirection of emotions from a PAST important figure (often a parent) onto a person in the PRESENT (here the therapist). The patient's childhood feelings of paternal abandonment are reactivated toward the psychiatrist who canceled. Answer E.
strategy: Match the pattern: feelings tied to a past figure (unavailable father) resurface toward a current person (therapist) = transference. Reject other defenses: acting out (expressing impulses through behavior), displacement (redirecting emotion onto a less-threatening OBJECT, not re-experiencing a past relationship), projection (attributing one's own unacceptable feelings to another), and reaction formation (behaving opposite to one's true feelings). Distinguish from countertransference (the therapist's feelings toward the patient).

eliminations.label: Acting out - impulses via behavior
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: expressing unconscious feelings through inappropriate ACTIONS. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the patient verbalized a feeling rooted in his past relationship, he did not act out an impulse (e.g., breaking objects in rage). ✅ Correct if: a tantrum/impulsive destructive behavior expressing emotion.

eliminations.label: Displacement - onto a less-threatening object
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: redirecting a strong emotion from its source onto a safer target. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: transference specifically re-experiences feelings from a PAST relationship in the present; displacement would be, e.g., yelling at his kids instead of his father. ✅ Correct if: anger at the boss taken out on family.

eliminations.label: Projection - attributing own feelings to another
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: misattributing one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: he isn't disowning his own feeling and assigning it to the therapist; he is re-experiencing childhood abandonment. ✅ Correct if: 'you're disappointed in me' when he is actually disappointed in the therapist.

eliminations.label: Reaction formation - opposite behavior
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: transforming an unacceptable feeling into its opposite. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: he expressed the actual (negative) feeling, not its opposite (e.g., praising the therapist). ✅ Correct if: effusive gratitude masking anger.

reasoning: The patient recalls a father who was unavailable during childhood
When the therapist cancels, the childhood feelings of abandonment are reactivated
He redirects those past feelings onto the present-day therapist
mechanism: TRANSFERENCE is the unconscious SHIFTING of emotions, desires, and expectations associated with an important person from the PAST (frequently an early attachment figure such as a parent) onto a person in the PRESENT - classically the therapist. Here the patient's FATHER was emotionally unavailable in childhood; when the psychiatrist unexpectedly cancels a session, those old feelings of ABANDONMENT and unimportance are reactivated and re-experienced toward the psychiatrist ('you aren't there when I need you'). Transference can be positive or negative and is a central phenomenon in psychodynamic therapy. It is distinguished from COUNTERTRANSFERENCE (the therapist's feelings about the patient, based on the therapist's past). The distractors are different defense mechanisms: acting out (impulses via behavior), displacement (redirecting emotion onto a less-threatening object), projection (attributing one's own feelings to another), and reaction formation (expressing the opposite of a true feeling).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Behavioral science > transference vs countertransference; defense mechanisms (acting out, displacement, projection, reaction formation); transference = past feelings redirected onto therapist.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Childhood feelings about father reactivated toward the therapist = transference.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on transference vs countertransference, displacement, projection, or reaction formation? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Displacement = onto a safer object; projection = own feelings onto another; reaction formation = opposite behavior; acting out = impulsive behavior.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: transference = patient shifts PAST relationship feelings onto therapist; countertransference = therapist's feelings onto patient.
